title: Our Students Can Read the Words. Can They Read Between the Lines? https://theeducatorsroom.com/our-students-can-read-the-words-can-they-read-between-the-lines/
author: Greg Kyle
summary: Greg Kyle, a high school English and History teacher, argues that inference is the quiet skill behind deeper reading and that many students are not developing it. He starts from a classroom test in which only 28 percent of his learners earned full marks on an inference question, and cites PISA data showing that only about 7 percent of students reach the top reading proficiency levels. His central claim is that inference grows through rich language exposure and live conversation, and that fast, transactional online exchanges give students less practice with extended explanation. He notes that reading removes the visual and verbal cues that make conversation easy to interpret, so weak inference shows up sharply in exam-style reading. His remedies are teacher think-alouds, read-alouds that invite discussion, parents who give reasons rather than bare commands, and open prompts such as asking students to explain what could have happened in a picture of a fallen chair and scattered papers.
points: Inference draws on vocabulary, syntax, working memory and monitoring, so it has to be taught and modeled rather than assumed.
Giving the reason behind an instruction triggers inference in a way that a bare command does not, which makes everyday parenting and teaching talk a training ground.
Online exchanges can involve inference, but shorter transactional conversation may not transfer to the longer inferential demands of academic reading.
Reading aloud and teacher think-alouds restore the verbal clues that independent text withholds and reduce the cognitive load of building meaning.
Playful open prompts, like explaining a picture of a fallen chair, make inference enjoyable and build the habit of meaning-making.
quotes: The ability to infer meaning is multi-faceted. A reader must draw on vocabulary, context, language knowledge, syntax, working memory and the ability to monitor whether what they are reading makes sense.
It is not that only 7% of students are capable of inference, but that few reach higher levels of reading proficiency where a depth of understanding is shown.

Yet, more often, young people engage in conversation that consists of shorter exchanges designed to accomplish something quickly: ask a question, give an instruction, get an answer, react and move on.
When learners share verbal forms of conversation, they do so within a network of visual and gestural clues. Even the atmosphere of a group facilitates comprehension.

As parents, our first instinct is to adopt instructional language (do this, do that): it is both comfortable and necessary. But as a tool to shape inference, it is limited, and an explanation for decisions is better
The former breeds compliance while the latter triggers inference: there is a reason attached to instruction.
In a world increasingly carved for speed and brevity, meaning-making should be more than a curriculum objective.
